senses: A stew of beef or veal and vegetables, flavoured with paprika.
Synonym of American chop suey.
A style of play in which the cards are not thoroughly shuffled between consecutive deals, so as to make the suits less evenly distributed between the players.
A hodgepodge, mishmash
ety: From French goulasch, itself from Hungarian gulyás (“herdsman”), an ellipsis of gulyáshús (“herdsman meat”), gulyásétel (“herdsman food”), and/or gulyástokány (“herdsman stew”). First attested in English 1866.

senses: A hut in the Italian mountains.
ety: From Italian rifugio. Doublet of refuge and refugium.

senses: Rough or lumpy.
examples: She was a little woman, in a bonnet and a black costume. Her bonnet was in its third year; it was a great grievance to Annie. “Mother!” the girl implored, “don’t wear that nubbly little bonnet.”
Though Clifford paid preliminary homage to them both, she was the one he finally made love to, rather quickly on the nubbly hooked rug.
When that crust is nubbly and evenly browned, and the chicken meat is cooked through, the chicken is sublime.

senses: A set of swings (hanging seats for children) attached to a frame.
Made of matter (as opposed to antimatter).
ety: From Middle English terrene, from Anglo-Norman terriene, feminine of terrien, from Latin terrēnus, from terra (“earth”).

senses: Resembling a sesame seed in size or shape.
Capable of being written.
To self-destruct.
A short-lived modernist movement in British art and poetry of the early 20th century, incorporating elements of cubism and futurism.
ety: From vortex + -ism, attributed to Ezra Pound.
examples: Much noise has been made by Vorticism, Futurism, Cubism, Vertiginism.

senses: The state or quality of being irreverent; want of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a superior.
ety: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.

senses: Capable of being resold.
A wrestling move in which the opponent's arm is held immobile.
Any of several distinct attacks against an opponent’s arm in martial arts.
A fighting hold in which the arm is used to immobilise an opponent.
Power to control or heavily influence something or someone.
examples: It would keep the bone-cage of his body safe: no enemy's clasp would crush him in it, no vicious armlock choke his life out.

senses: A person in a large business whose task is to maximize profits and make the business more efficient.
The design, organization, and management of museums.
Resembling a stream; streamlike.
Full of streams.
Abounding with snow; snowy; snow-covered (now especially in reference to plant habitats).
ety: From Latin nivalis, from nix, nivis (“snow”).

senses: Situated or occurring on the summit of a mountain.
A person who fells trees; a lumberjack
A machine for felling trees.
A person who fells a seam.
An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam.
ety: From Middle English fellere, feller; equivalent to fell + -er.

senses: An immature bird.
ety: From cheep + -er, from the noise they make.

senses: An ionocraft.
One who builds bridges
One who bridges, or connects two previously separate things.
One who plays bridge (card game)
ety: From Middle English briggere, equivalent to bridge + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (agent noun suffix).
examples: And he wasn't an ordinary bridger, Tuck remembers, he was said to be one of the best bridge-masters on Pomperoy.

senses: Somebody who mines for gold.
A dyestuff extracted from certain lichens, that changes color when exposed to pH levels greater than or less than certain critical levels.
A simple test of acidity in a liquid using litmus, usually in the form of litmus paper.
A simple test of any attribute; a litmus test.
ety: From Middle English litmose, lytmose, litemose, from Old Norse litmosi (“moss used for dyeing”), from lita (“to dye, stain”) + mosi (“moss”), the former from litr (“colour, dye, blee”), from Proto-Germanic *wlitiz, *wlituz (“appearance, blee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to see”). Cognate with Old English wlite (“appearance, form, brightness, countenance”). More at moss.

Having or resembling yeast.
Foamy and frothy.
Emotionally bubbling over (as with exuberance)
Surrounding an apex (especially of a tooth).
Across or spanning the Antarctic (the continent of Antarctica and the sea ice of the Southern Ocean that meets its shores).
A liking for sentimental things.
An overly sentimental thing or condition; bathos or sentimentality.
A view according to which morality is somehow grounded in moral sentiments or emotions.
Any of several passerine birds, of the family Vangidae, from Madagascar.
A transverse ridge of bedrock that has been exposed by glacial erosion.
One who or that which hashes (in various senses).
A food service worker in a low-end establishment.
One who participates in a hash run; a hare or hound in hashing.
Precise in observance of legal or religious requirements; strict; overscrupulous; rigid (often used by way of reproach or contempt).
A monetary unit of Saudi Arabia equal to one hundredth of a riyal.
examples: This is annoying, but the difference in price is only a few halalas and arguing, in my experience, is pointless.

senses: A soap opera.
examples: In terms of its general mood, the average Australian soapie, in comparison with the American soap, is less intense, less subjective, and certainly a good deal less angst-ridden.
CHANNEL 7 has censored a lesbian kissing scene in its popular family soapie Home and Away after a viewer backlash.

senses: To make or set free; liberate; deliver; release.
ety: From Middle English *befreen, *bifreen, from Old English befrēoġan (“to free, liberate”); equivalent to be- + free. Cognate with West Frisian befrije (“to liberate”), Dutch bevrijden (“to liberate, deliver”), German befreien (“to set free, liberate”), Swedish befria (“to liberate, free, deliver”).
examples: Such is the fascinating future for Russia in the event of the establishment and welding of the befreed Russian Nation into a strong and firm democratic State.
They helped rather the big industrialists than to befree the poors from the yoke of the money-lenders.

senses: A portable personal compact disc player with headphones.
Not fully developed in mature animals.
Of a vestigial structure; that has lost all or most of its original function in the course of evolution.
ety: From Latin vestīgium + -al. By surface analysis, vestige + -ial.

senses: Sixteenth-century (1500s).
Someone who signals.
A device that sends a signal.
The amount that a room can hold, especially the number of people that can fit into a room.
The people in a room, considered as a group.
examples: Bengston doing a roomful of painting is like Joe Willie Namath doing a gameful of curl patterns, Jason Robards doing an eveningful of O'Neill, Tina Turner doing a concertful of. . . . and so on.
